source_refs.note: Book p. 276: 14.3.2 Parallel Vectors, u x v = 0 iff sin theta = 0 or a zero vector, cases (i), (ii) and the Note box on the zero vector.

blocks.text: If \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) are parallel vectors, then \((\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \sin 0 = 0)\).

items: (i) If \(\sin\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \theta = 0^{\circ}\) or \(180^{\circ}\). Which shows that the vectors \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) are parallel.

(ii) If \(\underline{u} = \underline{0}\) or \(\underline{v} = \underline{0}\), then since the zero vector has no specific direction, we adopt the convention that the zero vector is parallel to every vector.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Zero vector is both parallel and perpendicular to every vector. This apparent contradiction will cause no trouble, since the angle between two vectors is never applied when one of them is zero vector.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why \(180^{\circ}\) also counts as parallel: vectors pointing in exactly opposite directions lie along the same line (they are anti-parallel), and \(\sin 180^{\circ} = 0\) as well.
So the test is: two non-zero vectors are parallel exactly when \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = \underline{0}\).
Compare with 14.2: two non-zero vectors are perpendicular exactly when \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = 0\).
Example (ours): \(\underline{u} = \underline{i} + 2\underline{j} + 3\underline{k}\) and \(\underline{v} = 2\underline{i} + 4\underline{j} + 6\underline{k} = 2\underline{u}\) are parallel, and indeed the determinant formula of 14.3.5 gives \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = \underline{0}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Parallel vectors (\(\theta = 0^{\circ}\) or \(180^{\circ}\)) have \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = \underline{0}\).
2. For non-zero vectors: \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = \underline{0} \iff \underline{u} \parallel \underline{v}\).
3. The zero vector is taken as parallel (and perpendicular) to every vector.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = 0\) (the number) instead of \(\underline{0}\) (the zero vector).
2. Forgetting \(\theta = 180^{\circ}\): opposite vectors are parallel too.
3. Mixing the tests: dot product zero means perpendicular; cross product zero means parallel.
